opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to trust, and to what kind of work you want people to do.

When you set up a horse race, two or three teams work on the same problem and only one wins. That sounds efficient, since competition pushes everyone to go faster. But look at what it does to behavior. People stop sharing. If I find a trick that makes training more stable, why would I tell the team next door when we're racing each other? So you pay for the same lessons two or three times, and the organization as a whole learns more slowly. The losing team also often feels their work was wasted, and some good people get burned out or leave.

At Nvidia the culture is closer to this: here is the mission, here is the team that owns it, and we trust you to get it done. For us, the mission might be building world foundation models for physical AI, models that help robots and autonomous vehicles understand and simulate the physical world. Once a team owns that, the energy goes toward the problem itself rather than toward beating colleagues. When other groups have useful expertise, like systems, data, or simulation, they want to help, because there's no zero-sum game.

There's also a long-term argument. Research problems like generative models or world models aren't solved in one sprint. They need years of accumulated understanding: why a certain architecture fails, which data matters, how to evaluate something that's hard to measure. A team that owns the mission builds that depth. A horse race tends to reward whoever shows a good demo fastest, and that isn't always the approach that scales.

Jensen often talks about the mission being the boss. I find that very freeing as a researcher. You aren't optimizing for internal politics. You're asking what the right thing to build is and how to get there. If the direction is wrong, you correct it openly. You don't wait for some other team to win.

None of this means there's no pressure. The bar is very high, and the competition is real. It's just outside the company, not inside it. I'd rather have my team running hard against the problem and the rest of the world than against the people sitting next to us.

r001.rationale: The response says Nvidia assigns a team a mission and trusts it to deliver, while also emphasizing that the performance bar is very high.

r002.rationale: The response describes demanding research work and external competition, but does not present deliberately imposed hardship as a way to develop the team.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to how you treat people and how you treat compute.

When you run a horse race, you're telling two or three teams, "Go build the same thing, and in six months we'll pick a winner." On paper that sounds like healthy competition. In practice, what happens is that the people on each team know that most of them are going to lose. And when people know their work will likely be thrown away, they behave differently. They hoard information. They stop sharing what they learned about the data pipeline, or a trick that stabilized training, because sharing helps the competitor. You end up with three teams each discovering the same bugs independently. That's not competition, that's waste.

At Nvidia, the way Jensen runs things is more like: here is the mission, here is the team, you own it. If the model is bad, it's your problem, and you fix it. There's nobody else building the same thing down the hall. That creates a very different kind of pressure. It's not "beat the other team," it's "don't let the company down." And I actually find that pressure is more productive, because it's aligned with the outcome rather than with winning an internal game.

The second part is compute. Training a frontier model is extremely expensive. If you split your GPUs across three teams racing each other, every team gets one third of the budget, and none of them can do the experiment they really want to do. One team with the full budget can run the ablations properly, scale up properly, and actually learn what works. In this field, the scale of the experiment often determines whether you learn anything at all. So the horse race doesn't just cost you people's goodwill, it costs you the ability to do the science.

Now, I'm not saying there's no competition. There is, but it's external. We look at what the open models are doing, what the other labs are doing, and that's the race. Internally, I want people to feel like they're on the same side. When someone in another group finds something useful, I want them to walk over and tell us, not hide it.

And one more thing: ownership attracts a certain kind of researcher. The people who want to own a problem end to end, who want to be responsible for whether it ships, those are the people I want. A horse race selects for people who are good at playing the internal politics of winning the race, which is a different skill. I'd rather have the first kind.

r001.rationale: The response says the team is given a mission and ownership, and that if the model is bad, the team must fix it. This conveys trust paired with demanding performance expectations.

r002.rationale: The response describes pressure as productive, but does not present deliberately imposed hardship as a way to develop the entrusted team.

astra-6.text:
I prefer giving a team a clear mission because it aligns everyone around solving the problem. If you set up an internal horse race, people have two objectives: make the project succeed and beat the other team. Those objectives don’t always point in the same direction. You might hesitate to share an insight because it helps your competitor, even though sharing it would help the company.

When you entrust a team with a mission, the responsibility is clear. You’re saying, “We trust you to figure this out, and you’re accountable for the outcome.” That encourages people to take ownership, ask for help, and work across boundaries.

That doesn’t mean you should pursue only one technical idea. A team can test several approaches and debate them very rigorously. But the competition should be between ideas, with everyone learning from the results. I think that’s a better use of people’s energy than making teams compete for the right to continue their work.

r001.rationale: The response describes trust, a clear mission, and accountability for the outcome, but does not communicate demanding performance expectations.

r002.rationale: The response does not present deliberately imposed hardship as a way to develop the entrusted team.

sol-6.1.text:
I prefer giving a team a clear mission because it aligns everyone around solving the problem. In an internal horse race, you can create an incentive to beat the other team rather than share what you’ve learned. You may get several groups duplicating effort while keeping useful insights to themselves.

When one team owns the mission, the responsibility is clear, and people can put their energy into making it succeed. That doesn’t mean you only explore one idea. You can test competing approaches within the team, debate them rigorously, and change direction when the evidence tells you to. The competition should be between ideas, while the people work together.

r001.rationale: The response supports assigning a team a clear mission, but does not communicate trust paired with demanding performance expectations.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe imposing hardship to develop the entrusted team.
